Title: Saudi Arabia - Level 3: Reconsider Travel
Summary:
Reconsider travel

to Saudi Arabia due to risk of drone and missile targeting of American interests by Iran and the Iranian-supported Houthis, armed conflict, terrorism, exit bans, and local laws regarding social media activity. Some areas have increased risk. Read the entire Travel Advisory.

U.S. government employee travel restrictions

  • U.S. government employees working in Saudi Arabia require special authorization to use any airport in Saudi Arabia.
  • U.S. government employees working in Saudi Arabia are not allowed to travel within 20 miles of the Yemen border due to safety risks.
  • U.S. government employees working in Saudi Arabia need special authorization to travel to:
    • The cities of Qatif, Taif and Yanbu
    • The provinces of Jizan, Asir, and Najran.
  • U.S. citizens in Saudi Arabia are advised to take similar precautions.

Armed conflict

Following the onset of hostilities between the United States and Iran on February 28, 2026, there has been an ongoing threat of drone and missile attacks from Iran. Commercial flights are operational from Saudi Arabia, though they have been significantly disrupted at times.

Terrorism

There is risk of terrorist violence, including terrorist attacks and other activity in Saudi Arabia. Visit the U.S. Department of State’s country reports on terrorism to learn more.

Terrorism is a concern in Saudi Arabia. Attacks can occur with little or no warning, especially around holidays. They can involve knives, firearms, and vehicles.

Terrorists may use violence to respond to direct attacks against them or other military operations in the region.

Potential targets include:

  • Important political, cultural, or religious sites
  • Places visited by U.S. citizens and other foreigners
  • Tourist locations and large gatherings
  • Hotels and locations where U.S. citizens gather
  • Transportation hubs
  • Markets and shopping malls
  • Entertainment venues
  • Government facilities

Missile and drone attacks from Iran and threats from Houthis in Yemen

Iran and Iran-backed Houthi rebels have launched missile and drone attacks into Saudi Arabia.

  • Attacks have targeted cities, infrastructure, airports, military bases, diplomatic, and energy facilities throughout the country.
  • Iran-backed Houthi rebels have threatened to attack Saudi Arabia again.
  • Falling debris from intercepted drones and missiles are also a risk.
  • U.S. citizens living and working near energy infrastructure and military bases may be at increased risk, especially closer to the border with Yemen.
  • Do not photograph, film, or share information about missile or drone interceptions or impact sites. Saudi authorities have detained U.S. citizens for taking photos of recent events.

Exit bans

The Government of Saudi Arabia has imposed exit bans on some U.S. citizens that prevent them from leaving. These can last many years.   

  • Exit bans may be related to pending criminal and civil investigations and cases, including, but not limited to unpaid visa overstay fees, domestic family disputes, and other financial and labor disagreements.
  • In some cases, exit bans can continue even after a criminal sentence has been fully served or a private suit is settled.

Arbitrary Enforcement of Local laws

  • You are subject to Saudi Arabia’s local laws when traveling in the country. The U.S. government cannot guarantee your release if you are detained or arrested abroad.
  • If you break laws in Saudi Arabia – even by mistake – you could be deported, fined, imprisoned, or subject to an exit ban.
  • Some U.S. citizens have been detained for several months or even years without charges.
  • Saudi authorities may detain you if they consider your social media posts or other online activity to be critical, offensive, or disruptive to the public order.
  • Some U.S. citizens have been arrested for past social media activity, including comments posted while outside of Saudi Arabia. This may include posting, re-posting, or liking comments critical of the Saudi government or its leaders and policies. This also may apply to comments about public life or religion in Saudi Arabia.
  • Local laws against cybercrime and terrorism may be used to prosecute cases related to social media use.
  • Punishment for social media activity has included prison sentences of up to 45 years. Local authorities may not consider when, where, or in what context posts are made.

Aviation safety

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued a Notice to Airmen (NOTAM) or a Special Federal Aviation Regulation (SFAR). This is due to risks to civil aviation operating within or nearby Saudi Arabia. For more information, U.S. citizens should consult the Federal Aviation Administration’s Prohibitions, Restrictions and Notices.

Private car, train, and bus options may provide alternatives to air travel. Below are some transportation resources for your consideration. Please confirm availability and schedules directly with the providers.

  • Saudi Arabia Railways
  • SAT Transportation
  • SAPTCO

Do Not Travel to the Yemen border due to terrorism.

Title: Yemen - Level 4: Do Not Travel
Summary:
Do not travel

in Yemen due to risk of terrorism, unrest, crime, health risks, kidnapping, and landmines.

Do not travel to Yemen for any reason, including the island of Socotra. The U.S. Embassy in Sana’a suspended its operations in February 2015. The U.S. government cannot offer emergency services to U.S. citizens in Yemen due to the safety risks.

Terrorism

The Department of State re-designated Ansarallah, commonly referred to as the Houthis, as a Foreign Terrorist Organization in March of 2025.

  • Other terrorist groups also plan and carry out attacks in Yemen. These include Al-Qa'ida in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP) and Islamic State affiliates.
  • Terrorists may attack with little or no warning and may target:
    • Public sites
    • Places of worship
    • Transportation hubs
    • Markets
    • Government buildings and facilities

There is high risk of terrorist violence, including terrorist attacks and other activity in Yemen. Visit the U.S. Department of State's country reports on terrorism to learn more.

Review our information on Terrorism and Travel to High-Risk Areas.

Unrest

A civil war continues in Yemen. Yemen faces instability and the Houthis have repeatedly clashed with Yemeni government forces. The Houthis have launched missile and drone attacks against Yemeni government personnel, as well as civilians and infrastructure across the country since July 2026. The Houthis have also targeted infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and shipping in the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandeb.

  • Do not rely on significant assistance from local authorities.
  • Foreigners are frequently targets of kidnapping and carjacking, especially outside of urban areas.
  • Have a plan to leave in an emergency that does not depend on U.S. government help. Review our information on Crisis and Evacuations.
  • Military conflict has destroyed basic infrastructure like housing, medical facilities, schools, and utilities. This makes it hard to get electricity, clean water, and medical care. Humanitarian groups face obstacles in delivering food, medicine, and water.

Crime

Violent and organized crime is common in Yemen. Local law enforcement may not be able or willing to respond to serious crimes.

Health

Medical services for routine and emergency procedures in Yemen are limited and poor. There is a re-emergence of diseases like cholera, polio, and measles which are spreading in Houthi-controlled areas. Medicine and medical supplies are hard to find. Adequate medical treatment for routine and emergency procedures is often not available. If you decide to travel to Yemen:

  • Read the Health section of the Travel Guidance on this page for more information.
  • Visit the CDC’s Travel Health page for the latest information.

Kidnapping

U.S. citizens, especially dual U.S.-Yemeni citizens, are at high risk of kidnapping and detention in Yemen.

  • Young U.S. citizens may be kidnapped or trafficked for forced marriage. Family members in the United States or Yemen are often involved in these kidnappings.
  • The Houthis control Sana’a. They have detained U.S. citizens without cause, including some with dual citizenship.
  • U.S. citizens have faced difficulty and delays when trying to leave Yemen.

Review our information on U.S. Citizens Missing Abroad and for Victims of Crime.

Landmines

Landmines and unexploded ordnance exist throughout Yemen. Their location is often not marked or easy to recognize.

Socotra Island

Do not travel to Socotra Island or any part of Yemen. Some companies outside Yemen have misrepresented the safety of the Yemeni island of Socotra.

  • They offer tourist trips with unofficial and invalid "visas."
  • These companies put tourists in danger and legal jeopardy.
  • Only the Republic of Yemen government can issue valid Yemeni visas.

The U.S. government cannot help U.S. citizens in Socotra.

Aviation safety

Limited commercial flights are available from Aden to other airports in the region. Sana’a International Airport is closed for commercial flights as it is frequently the target of attacks due to its illicit use by the Houthis. Check with airlines and travel companies for the latest flight information.

Due to risks to civil aviation operating within or in the vicinity of Yemen, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued a Notice to Airmen (NOTAM) and a Special Federal Aviation Regulation (SFAR) prohibiting operations within the Sana’a Flight Information Region (FIR). For more information, U.S. citizens should consult the Federal Aviation Administration’s Prohibitions, Restrictions, and Notices.

Maritime travel

Due to risks to commercial shipping operating within or in the vicinity of Yemen territorial waters, the Department of Transportation’s Maritime Administration (MARAD) has issued a Maritime Advisory. For more information, mariners and passengers planning travel to Yemen should check the following:

  • U.S. Maritime Advisories
  • U.S. Maritime Alerts
  • Maritime Safety Office Navigational Warnings
  • U.S. Coast Guard Maritime Commons

The U.S. Coast Guard determined Yemeni ports do not have effective anti-terrorism measures. Vessels that arrive in U.S. ports from Yemeni ports must meet additional U.S. Coast Guard conditions of entry as described in the current Port Security Advisory, International Port Security Program - Port Security Advisory.

Mariners and passengers traveling through the ports of Yemen should exercise caution.

Title: Curaçao - Level 1: Exercise Normal Precautions
Summary:
Exercise normal precaution

in Curaçao.

Curaçao is generally a safe destination for travelers. 

  • Petty crime is most likely to occur in popular tourist locations. Stay aware of your surroundings. 
  • Most crimes against foreigners are crimes of opportunity, such as theft of unsecured property or vehicle break-ins. 
  • Beware of overcharges and scams in tourist areas. Some sellers may be aggressive. Most sites have tourist police available to help in uncomfortable situations. 
  • Crime rates are low. However, armed robberies occur at businesses storing large amounts of cash or involved in drug or gang activity. 
  • It is illegal to bring guns, ammunition, and even spent shells or casings into Curaçao. You may face arrest and detention for long periods of time.  
  • Review our Travel Guidance for Curaçao to learn how to prepare for a safe trip.

Title: Hong Kong - Level 2: Exercise Increased Caution
Summary:
Exercise increased caution

when traveling to the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (SAR) due to the arbitrary enforcement of local laws.

Exercise increased caution due to the arbitrary enforcement of local laws.

  • Hong Kong SAR authorities have passed laws that limit people’s civil liberties. The laws apply to anyone in Hong Kong, including foreigners. Authorities have also issued arrest warrants for individuals, including U.S. citizens, located outside of Hong Kong for activities undertaken overseas.
  • U.S. government employees must follow the policies established by their Department or Agency regarding official or personal travel to China, including to Hong Kong SAR.

National security laws and restriction of civil liberties

Since 2020, Hong Kong SAR authorities have taken away many freedoms from people living there.

On June 30, 2020, China imposed the Law on Safeguarding National Security in the Hong Kong SAR. On March 23, 2024, Hong Kong passed another similar law. Both laws list many crimes that are vaguely defined. The crimes include:

  • Trying to break apart China (acts of secession)
  • Working against the government (subversion)
  • Terrorism
  • Working with other countries against China (collusion with foreign entities)
  • Betraying the country (treason)
  • Stealing government secrets
  • Insurrection
  • Sabotage against public infrastructure
  • External interference

On March 23, 2026, the Hong Kong government changed the implementing rules relating to the Hong Kong National Security Law. It is now a criminal offense in national security cases to refuse to give the Hong Kong police passwords or not assist in decryption to allow authorities full access to all personal electronic devices, including cellphones and laptops. 

This legal change applies to everyone, including U.S. citizens, in Hong Kong, upon arrival, or just transiting Hong Kong International Airport. In addition, the Hong Kong government also has more authority to take and keep any personal devices, as evidence, that they claim are linked to national security offenses.

China applies its national security laws to everyone in Hong Kong SAR, including foreigners. China may also attempt to apply these laws to people who do not live in Hong Kong – including U.S. citizens and permanent residents.

If you say anything critical about China or Hong Kong SAR, you could be arrested, detained, kicked out, or prosecuted.

Hong Kong SAR authorities have issued arrest warrants for people who live in other countries and are alleged to be violating these laws. This includes U.S. citizens and permanent residents living outside their jurisdiction. Hong Kong SAR authorities are offering cash rewards to anyone who gives information that helps them arrest these people if they come to Hong Kong SAR.

Dual nationality

The Hong Kong SAR government does not recognize dual nationality. Dual U.S.-Chinese citizens and U.S. citizens of Chinese descent may be subject to additional security procedures and harassment. If you are a dual U.S.-Chinese citizen and enter Hong Kong SAR on a U.S. passport, and you are detained or arrested, Chinese authorities must notify the U.S. Embassy or a U.S. Consulate General of your detention. They must allow U.S. consular officials to have access to you.

Even if you enter on a U.S. passport, U.S. consular officers may not have access to you. For more information, visit Consular Protection and Right of Abode in HK(SAR) for Dual Nationals – U.S. Consulate General Hong Kong & Macau.

Demonstrations

Participating in demonstrations or other activities that authorities interpret as constituting an act of secession, subversion, terrorism, or collusion with a foreign country could result in criminal charges under the 2020 Hong Kong National Security Law, the 2024 Safeguarding National Security Ordinance, or other legal provisions. Be aware of your surroundings and avoid demonstrations.

Title: China - Level 2: Exercise Increased Caution
Summary:
Exercise increased caution

in mainland China due to the arbitrary enforcement of local laws, the use of exit bans without a fair and transparent process under the law, and the risk of unjust arrest or detention. Some areas have increased risk. Read the entire Travel Advisory.

Exercise increased caution in mainland China due to the arbitrary enforcement of local laws, the use of exit bans without a fair and transparent process under the law, and the risk of unjust arrest or detention.

Expansive national security, counterespionage, and data security laws grant Chinese officials broad discretion to detain or interrogate foreign nationals. This places U.S. citizens at risk for conducting even routine business, research, or expression in the public domain.  

The following may be targeted by Chinese authorities: 

  • U.S. citizens of Chinese heritage or origin
  • Anyone involved in business disputes or who has ties to U.S. corporate entities involved in business disputes in China
  • Anyone with a current or prior affiliation with U.S. law enforcement, U.S. military, or U.S. intelligence agencies
  • Anyone traveling on U.S. government-funded programs
  • Individuals with current or former connections to the U.S. government 

Ability to provide emergency consular services in some regions, especially in the Tibet Autonomous Region, is severely limited.  

U.S. government employees must follow the policies established by their Department or Agency regarding official or personal travel to China.  

Exercise increased caution in the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (SAR) due to the arbitrary enforcement of local laws.  

Reconsider travel to Macau Special Administrative Region (SAR) due to a limited ability to provide emergency consular services. Exercise increased caution due to the arbitrary enforcement of local laws.

  • Review specific risks and conditions in each jurisdiction.

Mainland China – Level 2:  Exercise Increased Caution

Arbitrary enforcement of local laws

The government of China arbitrarily enforces local laws. It may issue exit bans on U.S. citizens and citizens of other countries without fair and transparent processes under the law.

National security laws

Chinese law includes an expansive definition of national security and grants Chinese officials with broad discretion to portray a wide range of documents, data, statistics, or materials as “state secrets,” including retroactively.

These laws and other regulations may place foreign nationals at risk for conducting routine research or handling data that is publicly or commercially available to Chinese nationals. U.S. citizens in China may face detention without information about their alleged crimes or access to U.S. consular services. U.S. citizens in China may also face interrogations and detention without fair and transparent treatment under the law.  

U.S. citizens and other foreigners in China have faced interrogation, detention, and expulsion for alleged violations of national security laws. This includes, but is not limited to: 

  • individuals with current or previous relationships with U.S. law enforcement, U.S. military, U.S. intelligence agencies, or other agencies of the U.S. government;
  • individuals on U.S. government-funded programs;
  • business people;
  • former foreign-government personnel;
  • academics;
  • relatives of Chinese citizens involved in legal disputes;
  • journalists. 

Local authorities have detained and charged U.S. citizens involved in civil business disputes with criminal offenses under these laws. In some cases, U.S. citizens have been able to secure release by settling legal disputes in favor of Chinese businesses. 

In addition to their ability to detain and prosecute foreign nationals for alleged espionage and/or national security violations, authorities in China are also authorized to prevent foreign nationals suspected of engaging in so-called espionage activities from leaving China. 

China has disproportionately targeted U.S. citizens of Chinese heritage or naturalized U.S. citizens of Chinese descent for espionage investigations. This is particularly common for those with previous employment or other relationships with the U.S. government. 

People accused of violating national security laws, including espionage, are often denied access to a lawyer. There is increased official scrutiny of U.S. and third-country firms operating in China, such as professional service and due diligence companies. China’s security services have detained U.S. citizens, who have faced prosecution, including for conducting academic and business research or accessing publicly available material inside China.

Wrongful detention and exit bans

The Secretary of State has determined that China is wrongfully detaining some U.S. citizens. China has also used restrictions on travel or departure from China, referred to as “exit bans,” to:

  • force people to participate in government and Chinese Communist Party (CCP) investigations;
  • resolve civil disputes in favor of Chinese citizens; 
  • pressure family members or associates of a restricted person to return to China from abroad, even if the family member is estranged or the associate is no longer in contact with the restricted person;
  • gain bargaining leverage over foreign governments.

U.S. citizens might only become aware of an exit ban when they attempt to depart China. There may be no available legal process to contest an exit ban in a court of law. 

Security services and investigative agencies have imposed exit bans using non-transparent CCP-led processes outside of the court system. Chinese authorities have placed exit bans on individuals, including U.S. citizen minor children, whose relatives are under investigation by Chinese authorities, to compel them to return to China. 

In some cases, the Chinese government has told U.S. citizens that the exit bans will only be lifted if they provide certain testimony, even if the U.S. citizens state that the testimony would be false. 

The U.S. Embassy has received reports from U.S. citizens of being forced to sign statements Chinese officials know to be untrue. In multiple cases, exit bans related to civil or business disputes have remained in place for years. These exit bans have prevented U.S. citizens from obtaining needed medical treatment outside of China.   

Dual nationals and U.S. citizens of Chinese heritage

China does not recognize dual nationality. The Chinese government claims to represent the interests of all ethnic Chinese individuals all over the world, regardless of nationality. 

Dual U.S.-Chinese citizens, former Chinese citizens, those who hold Taiwan travel documents, and U.S. citizens of Chinese descent may be subject to additional scrutiny and harassment. 

If you hold a Chinese identity card (身份证 shenfenzheng), Chinese residency book (户口本 hukouben), or enter China on a Chinese-issued travel document (台胞证 taibaozheng or 旅行证 luxingzheng), Chinese authorities may consider you to be Chinese only and not recognize your U.S. citizenship. They may restrict or prohibit U.S. consular assistance if you are subject to an exit ban, emergency, disappearance, arrest, or detention. This includes minor children.

If you are a U.S. citizen and choose to enter mainland China on travel documents other than a U.S. passport and are arrested or detained, the Chinese government is not obligated to notify the U.S. Embassy or the U.S. Consulates General, or to allow consular access.  You may still request notification to the closest U.S. embassy or consulate, but the Chinese government is not required to provide it. 

Dual nationals and naturalized U.S. citizens of Chinese descent are strongly encouraged to enter China using a U.S. passport with an appropriate Chinese visa. The U.S. Embassy has received reports of authorities forcing dual nationals to enter China on their Chinese travel documents, or authorities refusing to recognize U.S. citizenship if a former Chinese national has not completed all steps to formally renounce their Chinese citizenship.

U.S. citizens who were formerly Chinese citizens may be required to complete additional bureaucratic steps before being allowed to leave the country. They may also face increased scrutiny of previous professional and personal actions while they held Chinese citizenship, including past or current business dealings. 

U.S. citizens who were formerly Chinese citizens may also face departure restrictions.  Former Chinese citizens who have not formally renounced or canceled their Chinese citizenship are often compelled to cancel their household registration and relinquish rights to social welfare programs before exiting China. 

The Chinese government has imposed exit bans while denying claims of U.S. citizenship for natural born and naturalized (non-dual) U.S. citizens of Chinese descent who entered China using a U.S. passport.

Communication and expression

Assume that China’s security services can read your emails, texts, and social media posts if you send them to or from China. 

Assume they can also read your messages if you use Chinese apps, even when you are in another country, including the United States.  

  • Security personnel could detain or deport U.S. citizens for sending private electronic messages critical of the government of China, Hong Kong SAR, or Macau SAR or the CCP. 
  • China has detained people even when they sent these messages outside of China. 
  • All universities and schools in China are controlled by the CCP. If foreign teachers or students in China express ideas contrary to what the Communist Party believes, they could be deported or detained. 

The government of China strictly manages the religious activities of foreigners. Foreigners wishing to hold collective religious services must abide by Chinese laws. Religious exchanges between foreigners and Chinese religious institutions are controlled by national or provincial religious associations. There are restrictions on the transport of religious materials to China. U.S. citizens conducting collective religious services have reported interference by Chinese authorities. Foreign citizens engaging in proselytizing, distributing religious materials, or conducting religious services or education with Chinese citizens without prior approval is strictly prohibited and may result in fines, detention, or deportation.

Drugs

Do not use illegal drugs in China or before you go to China. 

If you test positive for drugs, even if the drug was legal elsewhere, Chinese police can detain you right away. You could be fined, deported, or banned from ever coming back. 

Chinese authorities may force you to give blood, urine, or hair samples for drug testing. Penalties for illicit drug offenses such as importation, possession, or consumption are severe. 

Guns and munitions

China has extremely strict laws about weapons and ammunition. If you break these laws, even by mistake, you could go to prison. 

  • Before you travel to China, carefully check all your bags, backpacks, and luggage. Make sure there are no bullets, guns, or any pieces of ammunition inside – not even empty bullet casings or small parts.
  • If you hunt or shoot guns, do not use those same bags when you travel to China. Use different bags that have never been used for hunting or shooting.  
  • Be very careful and follow all Chinese laws about weapons. Breaking these laws can get you in serious trouble. 
Demonstrations

Do not join protests or demonstrations in China. 

Chinese authorities have very broad laws about what counts as a crime against the government. If you join a demonstration or any other activities that authorities interpret as against China, you could be arrested and charged of serious crimes. 

This includes things the government sees as: 

  • Trying to break apart China (act of secession)
  • Working against the government (subversion)
  • Terrorism
  • Working with another country against China (collusion with a foreign country) 

Stay aware of your surroundings and avoid demonstrations.

Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region and Tibetan Autonomous Prefectures

Extra security measures, such as security checks and increased levels of police presence and surveillance, are common in the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region and Tibetan Autonomous Prefectures. 

Authorities may impose curfews and travel restrictions on short notice.

Tibet Autonomous Region

China has severely restricted U.S. consular officers from traveling to the Tibet Autonomous Region.

This decision by China severely limits the ability of the U.S. embassy to provide consular services to U.S. citizens in Tibet. This includes emergency situations such as natural disasters or injury while engaged in mountain sports. 

The U.S. government has limited information about medical or emergency services in the Tibet Autonomous Region.

Extra security measures, such as security checks and increased levels of police presence and surveillance, are common in the Tibet Autonomous Region.

Authorities may impose curfews and travel restrictions on short notice.

If you decide to travel to the Tibet Autonomous Region:
  • Enroll in Smart Traveler Enrollment Program (STEP) to get important updates and alerts from the U.S. embassy or consulate. Enrolling helps the U.S. embassy or consulate contact you or your emergency contact in an emergency.
  • Enter China on your U.S. passport with a valid Chinese visa and keep it with you.
  • Read the destination information page for Mainland China.
  • Check with the Embassy of the People’s Republic of China in the United States for the most updated information on Chinese government requirements for travel to China. 
  • Review the China Country Security Report.
  • Visit the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) website for the latest Travel Health Information for China.
  •  Whether you are a first-time or frequent traveler, use the International Traveler’s Checklist.
  • We highly recommend that you buy travel insurance before you travel. Check with your travel insurance provider about evacuation assistance, medical insurance, and trip cancellation coverage.
  •  Be aware that U.S. citizens and U.S. Lawful Permanent Residents (LPRs) with Chinese heritage or with a connection to the United States government may be targeted for harassment, arrests, detention, or exit bans.
  • Avoid demonstrations.
  • Avoid communicating, either privately or publicly, opinions or observations that might be considered embarrassing or otherwise negative about China or the Chinese authorities.
  • Exercise caution near large gatherings or protests.
  • Avoid taking photographs of protesters or police without permission.
  • Keep a low profile.
  •  If you are arrested or detained, ask police or prison officials to notify the U.S. Embassy in Beijing immediately.
  • Do not consume illegal drugs in China or before going to China.
  • Do not bring any bullets, cartridges, weapons, munitions, or even remnants of or partial munitions to China.
  • Follow U.S. Embassy Beijing on X, WeChat, and Weibo.

Exercise increased caution in Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (SAR) due to the arbitrary enforcement of local laws.

Reconsider travel to Macau Special Administrative Region (SAR) due to a limited ability to provide emergency consular services. Exercise increased caution due to the arbitrary enforcement of local laws.

Title: Nepal - Level 2: Exercise Increased Caution
Summary:
Exercise increased caution

in Nepal due to natural disasters. Some areas have increased risk. Read the entire Travel Advisory.

Nepal regularly experiences earthquakes, floods, and landslides. Earthquakes can happen suddenly with little warning, including in the Kathmandu Valley.

During the monsoon season from June to September, heavy rain can cause flash floods and landslides. These can block roads, damage buildings, and make it hard to get help in an emergency.

Review our information on Weather and Natural Disasters in Nepal.

Emergency services

Medical services have limited ability to handle regular and emergency care. Review the Health section of the Travel Guidance on this page for more information.

Hospitals in Kathmandu are usually better than in other areas, but they can be crowded, may lack some equipment or medicines, and often ask that you pay before treatment. Medical treatment of foreigners is not paid for by the Government of Nepal.

Bring the medicines you need, get travel health insurance that covers medical evacuation, and understand you might need to go to another country for serious treatment. 

Do not travel to:

  • The Rasuwagadhi-Timure-Syafrubesi area of Rasuwa district, including the Nepal-China border crossing, for any reason due to flood damage, disrupted transportation and communications, search-and-rescue and recovery operations, and the risk of additional flooding and landslides.

Title: Peru - Level 2: Exercise Increased Caution
Summary:
Exercise increased caution

in Peru due to risk of crime, unrest, kidnapping, and terrorism. Some areas have increased risk. Read the entire Travel Advisory. 

  • U.S. government employees working in Peru need special authorization to travel to the Colombia-Peru border area in the Loreto Region due to safety risks. 
  • U.S. government employees working in Peru need special authorization to travel to the Valley of the Apurímac, Ene, and Mantaro Rivers (VRAEM), due to safety risks. 
  • U.S. government employees working in Peru need special authorization to travel to the VRAEM’s boundary cities of Abancay, Ayacucho, Huancavelica, and Huancayo due to safety risks.   
  • Review our information on Travel to High-Risk Areas. 

Crime  

Crime is common in Peru.  

  • Petty theft, carjackings, muggings, assaults, and other violent crime often happen even in daylight hours and with many witnesses around.   
  • Although rare, “express kidnappings,” where the victim is taken to a banking institution and forced to remove funds from their own accounts, may occur.  
  • The risk of crime increases at night.   
  • Criminal groups sometimes set up roadblocks to rob people in areas outside of Lima. 

Unrest 

Demonstrations occur regularly throughout the country. Public demonstrations can take place for political and economic issues.    

  • Demonstrations can shut down local roads, trains, and major highways. This often happens without warning or clear information on reopening times.   
  • Road closures can limit access to public transportation and airports.   
  • Closures may also disrupt travel in and between cities. 

Restrictions for U.S. government employees 

Due to road safety risks, U.S. government employees working in Peru are prohibited from nighttime driving. The only exception is within cities, between Lima and Huacho (to the north), and Lima and Paracas (to the south).   

  • U.S. government employees working in Peru may travel at night with commercial bus companies along the Pan-American Highway, to Huaraz, and on the Lima-Arequipa-Cusco corridor.    

Terrorism 

There is risk of terrorist violence, including terrorist attacks and other activity in Peru. Visit the U.S. Department of State's Country Reports on Terrorism to learn more.   

Kidnapping 

Kidnapping in Peru, which could lead to prolonged detentions for ransom, are relatively uncommon but remains a notable security concern.  Visitors should remain aware of their surroundings.   

Other 

U.S. travelers should not consume Ayahuasca or Kambo because of the known dangers.  U.S. citizens have suffered serious illness and, in some cases, died after taking these drugs. They have also been sexually assaulted, injured, or robbed while under the influence of these substances. Ayahuasca or Kambo consumption centers are located throughout Peru, including the jungle regions of Iquitos, Tarapoto, and Pucallpa, and tourist areas such as Cusco. 

U.S. citizen travelers should not use coca products (such as tea or candy). They are often offered as a remedy for high elevation symptoms but are considered a controlled substance and can interact with other medications. 

Do Not Travel to the Colombia-Peru border area in the Loreto Region due to crime. 

Do Not Travel to the Valley of the Apurímac, Ene, and Mantaro Rivers (VRAEM), which includes Vilcabamba, due to crime and threats of terrorism.   

Do Not Travel to Abancay, Ayacucho, Huancavelica, and Huancayo within the regions of Ayacucho, Cusco, Huancavelica, and Junín, due to crime and threats of terrorism.    

Note: The City of Cusco and popular tourist sites nearby, like the Sacred Valley, the Inca Trail, and Machu Picchu, are not located in the affected area.

Title: Tajikistan - Level 2: Exercise Increased Caution
Summary:
Exercise increased caution

in Tajikistan due to the risk of terrorism, unexploded landmines, and limited ability to assist U.S.-Tajik dual nationals.  Some areas have increased risk. Read the entire Travel Advisory..

 

Terrorism 

There are terrorist organizations in the region.  There is risk of terrorist violence, including terrorist attacks and other activity in Tajikistan. Visit the U.S. Department of State’s country reports on terrorism to learn more. 

Landmines and unexploded ordnances 

Unexploded landmines and cluster munitions are a hazard along the Afghan-Tajik and Uzbek-Tajik borders, the Vakhsh and Rasht valleys, and in the popular hiking area of Romit.  

  • Pay close attention to land mine warning signs.  
  • Do not venture off the road into areas marked with red and white plastic tape for any reason. 
  • Avoid roadside ditches, shoulders, and unmarked trails in these regions.  
  • Never touch anything resembling unexploded munitions. 

Some unmarked landmines may also be present in the Surobad district of GBAO and the Sarazam district. 

U.S. government employee travel restrictions 

  • U.S. government employees working in Tajikistan are not permitted to travel between cities at night. 
  • U.S. government employees working in Tajikistan must obtain special authorization from the embassy security office to travel to border areas with Afghanistan due to safety risks. 
  • U.S. government employees working in Tajikistan must obtain special authorization from the embassy security office to travel to GBAO due to the potential for armed conflict, in addition to receiving a special permit from the Tajik government to enter GBAO. 

Dual nationals 

  • Tajikistan does not recognize dual nationality with the United States.  
  • If you are a dual U.S.-Tajik citizen or of Tajik descent, local authorities may single you out for extra questioning and harassment.  
  • Dual nationals may be denied access to U.S. consular officials while in detention. 

Reconsider travel to: 

  • Tajikistan’s border with Afghanistan due to terrorism. 
  • Gorno-Badakhshan Autonomous Oblast (GBAO) due to the potential for armed conflict.

Title: Bhutan - Level 1: Exercise Normal Precautions
Summary:
Exercise normal precaution

in Bhutan.

Bhutan is generally a safe destination for travelers. Medical services for routine and emergency procedures are limited, specifically in rural areas. Read the Health section of the Travel Guidance on this page for more information.  

Bhutan regularly experiences flooding, landslides, and wildfires. The country is also vulnerable to earthquakes. Review our information on Weather and Natural Disasters in Bhutan.  

Review our Travel Guidance for Bhutan to learn how to prepare for a safe trip.

Title: Macau - Level 3: Reconsider Travel
Summary:
Reconsider travel

to Macau SAR due to a limited ability to provide emergency consular services and arbitrary enforcement of local laws.

Reconsider travel to Macau SAR due to a limited ability to provide emergency consular services and arbitrary enforcement of local laws.

  • Reconsider travel due to limited ability for the U.S. government to provide emergency consular services. There are travel restrictions imposed on U.S. diplomatic personnel.
  • Reconsider travel due to arbitrary enforcement of local laws.
  • U.S. government employees must follow the policies established by their Department or Agency regarding official or personal travel to China, including to Macau SAR.

The U.S. government has a limited ability to provide emergency services to U.S. citizens in Macau SAR. This is due to China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs travel restrictions on U.S. diplomatic personnel.

Even in an emergency, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs requires all U.S. diplomatic personnel, including those accredited to Macau SAR, to apply for and receive visas before entering Macau SAR. This can take a week or longer. That delay can significantly limit the U.S. government’s ability to offer timely consular services in Macau SAR.

Dual nationality

The Macau SAR government does not recognize dual nationality. Dual U.S.-Chinese citizens and U.S. citizens of Chinese descent may face additional security checks and harassment. If you are a dual U.S.-Chinese citizen and enter Macau SAR on a U.S. passport, Chinese authorities must notify the U.S. Embassy or a U.S. Consulate General if you are arrested. They must also allow U.S. consular officials to have access to you.

However, even if you enter on a U.S. passport, U.S. consular officers may not be able to access you. For more information, visit Consular Protection and Right of Above in HK(SAR) for Dual Nationals – U.S. Consulate General Hong Kong & Macau.

Demonstrations

Participating in demonstrations or any other activities that authorities interpret as constituting an act of secession, subversion, terrorism, or collusion with a foreign country could result in criminal charges under local broad security laws. Be aware of your surroundings and avoid demonstrations.

Title: Philippines - Level 2: Exercise Increased Caution
Summary:
Exercise increased caution

in the Philippines due to crime, terrorism, unrest, and kidnapping. Some areas have increased risk. Read the entire Travel Advisory. 

Exercise increased caution due to terrorism and unrest associated with ongoing insurgent activities in certain rural and remote regions of Leyte, Mindoro, Negros, and Samar.

  • Foreign terrorist organizations actively recruit Americans to participate directly in terrorist activities and/or provide financial support.
  • Terrorists and armed groups have carried out kidnappings, bombings, and other attacks. They have targeted public areas such as tourist sites, markets, and local government facilities in the Philippines.  
  • Violent crimes are common. They include robberies, kidnappings, physical assaults, and homicides.  
  • Protests can turn violent or result in traffic jams and road closures. Local governments have limited capacity to respond.  
  • The Philippines regularly experiences typhoons, earthquakes, and volcanic eruptions. Review our information on Weather and Natural Disasters. 
Terrorism

There is risk of terrorist violence, including terrorist attacks and other activity, in the Philippines. Visit the U.S. Department of State's Country Reports on Terrorism to learn more. 

Do Not Travel to:

  • The Sulu Archipelago, including the southern Sulu Sea, due to the risk of crime, terrorism, unrest, and kidnapping.

  • Marawi City in Mindanao due to the risk of terrorism and unrest.

Reconsider Travel to: 

  • Certain other areas of Mindanao (see below) due to crime, terrorism, unrest, and kidnapping.

Title: Brazil - Level 2: Exercise Increased Caution
Summary:
Exercise increased caution

in Brazil due to crime and kidnapping. Some areas have increased risk. Read the entire Travel Advisory.

Crime

Violent crime occurs in urban areas, day and night.  Crimes include murder, armed robbery, and carjacking. 

  • Gang activity and organized crime are widespread. and are often tied to the illegal drug trade. 
  • Assaults are common, including with sedatives or drugs placed in drinks, especially in Rio de Janeiro. 
  • Criminals target foreigners through dating apps or at bars before drugging and robbing their victims. 

U.S. government employees working in Brazil need special authorization to travel to the following areas due to safety risks: 

- Within 100 miles/160 km of Brazil’s land borders (except travel to the Foz do Iguacu and Pantanal),

- informal housing developments in Brazil and,

- the Administrative Regions of Ceilandia, Santa Maria, Sao Sebastiao, and Paranoa between 6:00 p.m. and 6:00 a.m.

U.S. government employees are advised not to use municipal buses in Brazil due to serious risks of robbery and assault, especially at night.

Kidnapping 

Kidnapping for ransom involving U.S. citizens is rare but occasionally occurs. Brazilians are most often targeted, but foreigners remain vulnerable. U.S. businesses frequently arrange enhanced security for senior executives in São Paulo and other major cities. 

Organized criminal groups sometimes target individuals observed withdrawing money from ATMs or leaving banks. Use ATMs in secure locations such as shopping malls or major hotels. Express kidnapping — in which criminals force victims at gunpoint to withdraw cash from multiple ATMs or transfer funds via banking apps (commonly Pix) — is an ongoing threat to both locals and foreigners. 

To reduce your risk, vary your routes and travel times; park in well-lit, guarded garages, as criminals often confront victims at their vehicles; and limit the number of bank and credit cards you carry to reduce potential losses

Do Not Travel to:

  • International land borders due to crime and kidnapping. 
  • Informal housing developments (favelas, vilas, comunidades or conglomerados) due to crime.
  • Brasilia’s Satellite cities due to crime.

Title: Libya - Level 4: Do Not Travel
Summary:
Do not travel

to Libya for any reason due to crime, terrorism, health concerns, unrest, kidnapping, or landmines. Read entire Travel Advisory.

Do not travel to Libya for any reason.

Restrictions on U.S. Government Personnel Movement
  • There is currently no U.S. Embassy in Libya.
  • The U.S. government cannot offer emergency services to U.S. citizens in Libya due to the safety risks.
  • U.S. citizens in Libya in need of routine consular services should contact the U.S. Embassy in Tunis, Tunisia for assistance. 
Crime
  • Clashes among armed groups, including violence between competing armed groups and government-aligned forces, can occur at any time.
  • Weapons are plentiful in Libya and are controlled by various government organizations, armed groups, tribal factions, and criminal organizations.
  • Criminal organizations in Libya are known to be armed and involved in drug and human trafficking and other smuggling activity.
  • Targeted kidnappings and assassinations are common and committed by criminal organizations and armed groups.
  • Crimes of opportunity occur frequently. Wealthy or foreign nationals are often victims of these crimes.
Terrorism

There is risk of terrorist violence, including terrorist attacks and other activity in Libya. Visit the U.S. Department of State's country reports on terrorism to learn more.

  • Terrorist attacks could occur with little or no warning, targeting government facilities.
  • The Commandant of the U.S. Coast Guard has determined that effective anti-terrorism measures are not in place in Libyan ports and has imposed conditions of entry on vessels that arrive in U.S. ports having visited ports in Libya. Mariners and passengers traveling through the ports of Libya should exercise increased caution. 
  • Review our information on Terrorism. 
Health
  • Refer to our list of medical providers.
  • Make sure your insurance includes medical evacuation coverage.
  • Check with your doctor about required vaccines for high-risk exposure before you go to Libya.
  • Review the Health section in the Travel Guidance for Libya.
Unrest

Demonstrations related to the local political situation are common and may occur with little notice. Demonstrations may disrupt transportation and other essential services or lead to violence.

  • Even demonstrations intended to be peaceful can turn confrontational and escalate into violence.
  • Outbreaks of violence between protestors and government forces can occur with little warning and impact U.S. citizens.  
  • Avoid demonstrations and large crowds.
  • Check local media for breaking news. Be prepared to adjust your plans accordingly
  • U.S. citizens should always carry proof of citizenship and valid immigration status, but having these documents does not guarantee fair treatment.
  • Check local media for breaking news. Be prepared to adjust your plans.
  • During large-scale incidents of unrest, principal transportation options including highways, airports, and borders have been closed.
Kidnappings, Hostage-taking
  • Kidnapping is widespread, and victims have included U.S. citizens.
  • Kidnappers may take advantage of unprepared travelers.
  • Armed groups sometimes detain travelers for arbitrary reasons, do not grant detainees access to lawyers or legal processes, and do not allow detainees to inform others of their status.
  • Criminal or armed groups have detained and threatened to kill, injure, or continue to detain individuals in order to compel a third party (including a governmental organization) to do something as a condition of release.
  • Choose one family member to serve as the point of contact if you are kidnapped or taken hostage. That person can communicate with kidnappers or hostage-takers, media, U.S. or foreign government agencies, and members of Congress.
Other
Unexploded ordnance
  • Landmines and unexploded ordnance exist throughout Libya. The locations of landmines and unexploded ordnance are often not marked or easy to recognize.
  • Obey landmine warning signs. Do not venture off the road into areas marked with red and white plastic tape.  
  • Avoid roadside ditches, shoulders, and unmarked trails. Never touch anything resembling unexploded munitions.
Aviation safety
  • While there are airports in Libya with regular domestic and international flights, flights are often delayed, rerouted, and cancelled without warning.
  • The U.S. government prohibits U.S. commercial aviation operations within Libyan airspace.
  • Review the Transportation section regarding aviation safety oversight in the Travel Guidance for Libya.
  • The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued a Notice to Airmen (NOTAM) and a Special Federal Aviation Regulation (SFAR). This is due to risks to civil aviation operating within or nearby Libya. For more information U.S. citizens should consult the Federal Aviation Administration’s Prohibitions, Restrictions and Notices.

Title: Oman - Level 3: Reconsider Travel
Summary:
Reconsider travel

to Oman due to risk of armed conflict and terrorism. Some areas have increased risk. Read the entire Travel Advisory.

As of August 30, 2026, family members may join U.S. government employees who work in Oman.

Armed Conflict

Following the onset of hostilities between the United States and Iran on February 28, 2026, there has been an ongoing threat of drone and missile attacks from Iran.

Terrorism

There is risk of terrorist violence, including terrorist attacks in Oman.  Visit the U.S. Department of State’s country reports on terrorism to learn more.

Terrorism is a concern in Oman.  Attacks can occur with little or no warning, especially around holidays. They can involve knives, firearms, and vehicles.

Potential targets include:

  • Important political, cultural, or religious locations 
  • Places visited by U.S. citizens and other foreigners 
  • Tourist locations and large gatherings
  • Transportation hubs
  • Markets and shopping malls
  • Entertainment venues
  • Government facilities
  • Terrorists may use violence to respond to direct attacks against them or other military operations in the region.
Aviation Safety

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued an ongoing Special Federal Aviation Regulation and Notice to Airmen (NOTAM).  This is due to risks to civil aviation operating within or nearby Yemen.  For more information Americans should consult the Federal Aviation Administration’s Prohibitions, Restrictions and Notices.

Do Not Travel to the Yemen border area due to terrorism and armed conflict.

Title: Iraq - Level 4: Do Not Travel
Summary:
Do not travel

to Iraq due to terrorism, kidnapping, armed conflict, crime, health risks, and the U.S. government’s limited ability to provide emergency services to U.S. citizens in Iraq.

Do not travel to Iraq for any reason. The U.S. government has limited ability to offer emergency services to U.S. citizens in Iraq due to the safety risks.

The Iraqi government cannot guarantee the safety of U.S. citizens against sudden outbreaks of violence and armed conflict.

U.S. government employee travel restrictions 

The Department of State requires U.S. government personnel working in Iraq to live and work under strict security protocols due to serious threats.  

Due to safety risks, U.S. government employees need special authorization to travel to Iraq. Only family members who meet the following requirements may join U.S. government employees working in Iraq:

  • Are 21 years of age or older, and
  • Are employed by the U.S. government.

Kidnapping

U.S. citizens in Iraq face high risks, including violence and kidnapping.

Terrorism

There is a risk of terrorist violence, including terrorist attacks and other activity in Iraq.   Terrorists, including Iran-aligned militias and ISIS, encourage and conduct attacks against U.S. persons and interests in Iraq.  Visit the U.S. Department of State's country reports on terrorism to learn more.

Crime and armed conflict

Anti-U.S. militias threaten U.S. citizens and international companies.  Attacks using improvised explosive devices, indirect fire, and unmanned aerial vehicles occur in many areas, including major cities.  Targets of recent attacks have included hotels, universities, energy infrastructure, airports, and other locations perceived as affiliated with the United States, including diplomatic facilities.

Health

Emergency and intensive care facilities in Iraq are limited and likely unavailable outside of the largest cities.

If you need emergency medical assistance, hospitals, doctors, ambulances, and medical supplies may be low quality or unavailable.  Problems with transportation, roads, and safety can result in delays if you need medical evacuation.

Aviation safety

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued a Special Federal Aviation Regulation (SFAR) and a Notice to Airmen (NOTAM) prohibiting certain flights in the region.  This is due to risks to civil aviation operating within or near Iraq.

  • For more information U.S. citizens should consult the Federal Aviation Administration’s Prohibitions, Restrictions and Notices.

Title: United Arab Emirates - Level 3: Reconsider Travel
Summary:
Reconsider travel

to the United Arab Emirates due to terrorism and armed conflict. 

U.S. government employees working in the UAE need special authorization to travel to military bases and critical energy infrastructure sites due to UAE government restrictions and potential security risks. 

As of August 29, 2026, family members may join U.S. government employees who work in UAE.

Armed Conflict

Following the onset of hostilities between the United States and Iran on February 28, 2026, there has been an ongoing threat of drone and missile attacks from Iran and significant disruptions to commercial flights. The Iranian regime has publicly stated its intention to target locations in the UAE associated with the United States.

Terrorism

There is a risk of terrorist violence, including terrorist attacks and other activity in the United Arab Emirates. Visit the U.S. Department of State’s country reports on terrorism to learn more.

Terrorists may attack with little or no warning and may target tourist locations, transportation hubs, shopping areas, government facilities, places of worship, and in particular locations associated with the Jewish and Israeli communities.

Aviation Safety

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued an advisory Notice to Air Missions (NOTAM) or a Special Federal Aviation Regulation (SFAR).  This is due to risks to civil aviation operating within or nearby the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman region, including the UAE. For more information, Americans who plan to travel to the region should check the FAA’s Prohibitions, Restrictions and Notices.

Local laws

Residents and visitors should be aware the UAE has strict rules on social behavior, drug possession, traffic violations, financial crimes, and video recording officials, members of the public, infrastructure, or military activity. Breaking these rules can lead to arrest, fines, or an exit ban. Americans should review the Department of State’s Travel Guidances for UAE to learn about local laws, special circumstances, and additional information about travel to the United Arab Emirates.

Title: Jordan - Level 3: Reconsider Travel
Summary:
Reconsider travel

to Jordan due to terrorism and armed conflict. Some areas have increased risk. Read the entire Travel Advisory.

As of August 29, 2026, family members may join U.S. government employees who work in Jordan.

Armed Conflict

Following the onset of hostilities between the United States and Iran on February 28, 2026, there has been an ongoing threat of drone and missile attacks from Iran and significant disruptions to commercial flights.

Terrorism

There is a risk of terrorist violence, including terrorist attacks and other activity in Jordan. Visit the U.S. Department of State’s country reports on terrorism to learn more.

Terrorists may attack without warning, including such targets as:

  • Tourist locations;
  • Transportation hubs;
  • Markets and shopping malls;
  • Local government buildings.

Jordan is relatively stable but due to high tensions in the region, the security environment remains complex and can change quickly.

Zarqa City

There is heightened risk of terrorism and crime in Zarqa City.

  • All U.S. government personnel on official travel to this area must follow U.S. embassy travel restrictions. When traveling at night, U.S. government personnel on official travel must use major highways.
  • Personal travel by U.S. government personnel to these areas is allowed only during daylight hours. Direct transit through these areas is permissible at night along major highways.
Ma’an City and Ma’an Governorate

There is heightened risk of terrorism and crime in the following areas:

  • Ma’an city
  • All areas of Ma’an Governorate east of Highway 15 (“The Desert Highway”)
  • All areas of Ma’an Governorate within two kilometers to the west of Highway 15
  • All U.S. government personnel on official travel to these areas must follow U.S. embassy travel restrictions. When traveling at night, U.S. government personnel on official travel must use major highways.  
  • Personal travel by U.S. government personnel to these areas is allowed only during daylight hours. Direct transit through these areas is permissible at night along major highways. 
  • Review our information on Terrorism and Travel to High-Risk Areas.
Aviation Safety

For more information, Americans should consult the Federal Aviation Administration’s Prohibitions, Restrictions and Notices.

Do not travel to:

  • Mansheyat al Ghayyath, Ruwayshid, and the border with Syria and Iraq due to the risk of terrorism and unrest.
  • Designated Syrian refugee camps in Jordan due to the Government of Jordan’s restrictions on entry into these camps.
  • Rusayfah city due to the risk of terrorism and crime.
  • The Baqa’a neighborhood of Ayn Basha due to risk of terrorism and crime.

Title: Qatar - Level 3: Reconsider Travel
Summary:
Reconsider travel

to Qatar due to risk of armed conflict.

U.S. government employee travel restrictions 

As of August 28, 2026, family members may join U.S. government employees who work in Qatar.

Armed Conflict

Following the onset of hostilities between the United States and Iran on February 28, 2026, there has been an ongoing threat of drone and missile attacks from Iran and significant disruptions to commercial flights.

Aviation Safety

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued a Notice to Airmen (NOTAM) and/or a Special Federal Aviation Regulation (SFAR) for the region, including Qatar. This is due to risks to civil aviation from political and military tensions in the region.  The notice advises U.S. operators to review current threat information and to report safety or security incidents.  For more information, Americans should consult the Federal Aviation Administration’s Prohibitions, Restrictions and Notices.

Title: Kuwait - Level 3: Reconsider Travel
Summary:
Reconsider travel

to Kuwait due to the threat of armed conflict, landmines, and crime.

The U.S. government has limited ability to offer services to U.S. citizens in Kuwait due to safety risks.

U.S. government employee travel restrictions 
Due to safety risks, U.S. government employees need special authorization to travel to Kuwait. Only family members 18 years of age or older may join U.S. government employees working in Kuwait.

Armed conflict

Following the onset of hostilities between the United States and Iran on February 28, 2026, there has been an ongoing threat of drone and missile attacks from Iran. Commercial aviation has also been seriously disrupted.

Aviation safety

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued a Notice to Airmen (NOTAM) or a Special Federal Aviation Regulation (SFAR). This is due to risks to civil aviation operating within or nearby the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman region, including Kuwait. Consult the Federal Aviation Administration for the most up to date information on current FAA warnings.

Crime
  • Exercise increased caution in the Jleeb Al-Shuyoukh area in Kuwait City because of crime.
  • The Kuwaiti police report that the neighborhood of Jleeb Al-Shuyoukh near the Kuwait International Airport is a high-crime area.
Landmines
  • Landmines and unexploded ordnance exist in the desert area and some beaches north of the Mutla’a Ridge and near the border with Iraq.
  • The locations of landmines and unexploded ordnance are not marked, so it can be hard to know where they are.
  • There may be unexploded bombs, shells, and landmines left over from the 1990 Gulf War.
  • Do not travel to areas that are “off the beaten path.” Do not touch or move objects in those areas as they could explode.

Title: Ukraine - Level 4: Do Not Travel
Summary:
Do not travel

to Ukraine for any reason due to the Russia-Ukraine war.

U.S. embassy operations
  • The Embassy is open and operating in Kyiv; however, Embassy personnel are subject to movement, curfew, and activity restrictions, which may cause delays in provision of consular assistance to U.S. citizens outside of Kyiv.
  • U.S. citizens seeking assistance, including routine services, should email KyivACS@state.gov.
  • Review what the U.S. government can and cannot do to assist you in a crisis overseas.
U.S. government employee travel restrictions 
  • U.S. government employees need special authorization to travel outside of Kyiv due to safety risks.
  • Due to safety risks, the State Department does not authorize family members to join U.S. government employees in Ukraine.
  • U.S. citizens in Ukraine are advised to take the same precautions. 
Armed conflict

The Russia-Ukraine war continues, and non-frontline regions are also subject to Russian indiscriminate missile and drone attacks.

  • The security situation can change quickly, and travelers should be prepared to depart immediately with little to no warning.
  • Travelers should react to air alerts and seek appropriate shelter.
  • Closed airspace restricts travel options, and non-frontline regions are subject to martial law restrictions, such as a nationwide curfew.
  • U.S. government employees are subject to movement, curfew, and activity restrictions that may be more limited than Ukrainian government restrictions under martial law.
  • All U.S. citizens should carefully monitor U.S. government notices and local and international media outlets for information about changing security conditions and alerts to shelter in place.
  • U.S. citizens in Ukraine should stay vigilant and take appropriate steps to increase their security awareness in the event of military attacks.
  • Download and turn on notifications for free mobile applications – which U.S. government personnel in Ukraine are required to have and monitor – that announce air alerts in real time, such as Air Raid Siren and Alarm Map.
  • The U.S. Embassy does not have the ability to provide real-time alerts to the general U.S. citizen community of air threats.
  • Always know the location of your closest shelter.    
  • In the event of mortar, artillery, missile, drone, or rocket fire, follow instructions from local authorities and seek shelter immediately.
  • If you feel your current location is no longer safe, you should carefully assess the potential risks involved in moving to a different location.
State of emergency

On February 24, 2022, the Ukrainian government declared a state of emergency. Each region (oblast) decides on measures to be implemented according to local conditions.

Measures could include:

  • curfews
  • restrictions on freedom of movement
  • ID verification
  • increased security inspections
  • other measures
  • Follow any oblast-specific state of emergency measures.
Dual nationals

While Ukrainian law does allow dual nationality, Ukraine will not recognize your U.S. citizenship if you are also a citizen of Ukraine.

  • Dual citizens will be treated as Ukrainian citizens while in Ukraine and will be required to use a Ukrainian passport upon entry and exit of the country.
  • Men aged 23-60 with Ukrainian citizenship are also subject to exit restrictions and possible mobilization during the period of martial law.
  • The U.S. Embassy in Kyiv has received numerous reports of dual U.S.-Ukrainian citizens encountering significant difficulties both entering and exiting Ukraine.
  • Travelers with family ties to Ukraine should consult the nearest Ukrainian Embassy or Consulate regarding potential citizenship obligations before entering Ukraine.
  • For more information on traveling with dual nationality, please visit our Travelers with Dual Nationality page.
Aviation safety

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued a Notice to Air Missions (NOTAM) prohibiting U.S. aviation operations into, out of, within, or over Ukraine. For more information, U.S. citizens should consult the FAA’s Prohibitions, Restrictions, and Notices.

Title: Serbia - Level 2: Exercise Increased Caution
Summary:
Exercise increased caution

in Serbia due to crime.

Crime can occur anywhere in Serbia. Police may take longer to respond than they do in the United States.

Crime
  • Violence associated with organized crime and high-profile sporting events is common.
  • Petty crime is common, especially in popular tourist locations. Stay aware of your surroundings.
  • Most crimes against foreigners are crimes of opportunity, like purse snatching and pickpocketing.

Title: Ethiopia - Level 3: Reconsider Travel
Summary:
Reconsider travel

to Ethiopia due to unrest, crime, kidnapping, terrorism, landmines, communications disruptions, and exit bans. Some areas have increased risk. Read the entire Travel Advisory.

Unrest
  • The security situation in Addis Ababa is stable. However, there is sporadic violent, armed conflict, and civil unrest outside of Addis Ababa.
  • The security situation may worsen suddenly without warning.
Communications disruptions
  • Internet, cellular data, and phone services are often restricted or shut down before, during, and after unrest. 
  • These disruptions affect the U.S. embassy’s ability to communicate with Americans in Ethiopia and delay consular services.
Limited consular services for U.S. citizens
  • U.S. government employees working in Ethiopia need special authorization to travel to most locations outside of Addis Ababa due to safety risks.
  • Due to travel restrictions, the U.S. embassy has limited access to U.S. citizens arrested or detained in Ethiopia. Routine consular services are only available at the embassy.
  • Ethiopian law does not recognize dual citizenship. There are often delays in notifying the U.S. embassy of an arrest for dual U.S.-Ethiopia nationals. 
Exit bans that prevent departure
  • You are subject to local laws. If you break Ethiopian laws – even by mistake – you could face deportation, fines, imprisonment, or an exit ban. Exit bans prevent travelers from leaving.
  • As noted, Ethiopian law does not recognize dual citizenship. Research Ethiopian entry and exit requirements and immigration law if you travel. Dual citizens who have entered Ethiopia on their Ethiopian passports have been heavily fined after government authorities discovered they also held U.S. passports. Ethiopian law treats dual nationals as foreigners. Individuals who obtain their first U.S. passport while in Ethiopia, including children of U.S. citizens born in Ethiopia and documented with a Consular Report of Birth Abroad, should immediately obtain a visa or residency permit. 
  • The Ethiopian government imposes exit bans, including on minors, who have unpaid immigration fines and strictly enforces them.
  • There have been cases where U.S. citizens have been assessed more than $100,000 in immigration fines and prevented from leaving Ethiopia until they resolved the fines.
Crime
  • Petty crime is common, especially in popular tourist locations. Stay aware of your surroundings.
  • Most crimes against foreigners are crimes of opportunity, like purse snatching and pickpocketing.
  • Violent crime can occur and is more common after dark. Do not walk or drive at night. 
Terrorism
  • There is risk of terrorist violence, including terrorist attacks and other activity in Ethiopia. Visit the U.S. Department of State’s country reports on terrorism to learn more.
Kidnapping
  • Criminal and terrorist groups are active in Ethiopia and have targeted foreigners for kidnapping. 
  • The risk of kidnapping for ransom is highest in the following regions: 
  • Gambella 
  • Benishangul Gumuz 
  • Somalia border 
  • Sudan border
  • South Sudan border  
Landmines
  • Landmines and unexploded ordnance exist in the Somali region near the border with Somalia. The locations of landmines and unexploded ordnance are often not marked or easy to recognize.

Do Not Travel To:

  • Tigray region and border with Eritrea due to armed conflict, unrest, and crime.
  • Specific areas within the Afar region due to armed conflict, unrest, and crime.
  • Amhara region due to armed conflict, unrest, and crime.
  • Gambella region due to crime, ethnically motivated violence, kidnapping, armed conflict, and unrest.
  • Benishangul Gumuz region due to crime, kidnapping, armed conflict, and unrest.
  • The Oromia region, with the exception of Bishoftu and Bale Mountains National Park due to armed conflict, ethnically motivated violence, and unrest.
  • Specific areas within the Central Ethiopia Region due to unrest.
  • Specific areas within the South Ethiopia Region due to armed conflict and unrest.
  • Specific areas within the Southwest Ethiopia Region due to armed conflict and unrest.
  • Specific areas within the Somali region due to terrorism and unrest.
  • Border with Somalia due to terrorism, kidnapping, and landmines.
  • Borders with Sudan and South Sudan due to crime, kidnapping, unrest, and armed conflict.
  • Border with Kenya due to terrorism, armed conflict, and unrest.
  • Border area with Eritrea due to the possibility of armed conflict and unrest.

Title: Bahrain - Level 3: Reconsider Travel
Summary:
Reconsider travel

to Bahrain due to terrorism and armed conflict.

U.S. government employee travel restrictions 

Due to safety risks, U.S. government employees need special authorization to travel to Bahrain. Only family members 18 years of age or older may join U.S. government employees who work in Bahrain. 

Armed Conflict

Following the onset of hostilities between the United States and Iran on February 28, 2026, there has been an ongoing threat of drone and missile attacks from Iran and significant disruptions to commercial flights.

Terrorism

There is a risk of terrorist violence, including terrorist attacks and other activity in Bahrain. Visit the U.S. Department of State’s country reports on terrorism to learn more.  

Terrorist groups continue plotting possible attacks in Bahrain. Terrorists may attack with little or no warning. Targets may include tourist sites, transportation hubs, markets, shopping malls, and religious sites as well as government and military facilities.

Aviation Safety

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued an ongoing Notice to Airmen (NOTAM).  This is due to risks to civil aviation operating within or nearby the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman region, including Bahrain.  For more information Americans should consult the Federal Aviation Administration’s Prohibitions, Restrictions and Notices.
